title: Week 5–6 Quiz Material (Paging + Virtual Memory + Xinu Memory Manager)
notes: A virtual **page** is a logical block of a process’s virtual memory (virtual address space), while a **page frame** (frame) is a fixed-size unit of physical RAM that can hold one page.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
If a program references an **unmapped** virtual page, the MMU detects it and triggers a **page fault** (a trap to the operating system).
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
A **page fault** occurs when the MMU sees an unmapped page and causes the CPU to trap to the OS so the OS can bring the page into memory and update the mapping.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
Core page fault handling sequence: (1) pick a page frame + write victim to disk if needed, (2) fetch the referenced page into that frame + update the map, (3) restart the trapped instruction.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
The OS cannot implement truly **Optimal** replacement at runtime because it does not know the future (when each page will be referenced next), so Optimal is a benchmark not implementable.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
Common replacement algorithms include Optimal, NRU, FIFO, Second Chance, Clock, LRU, NFU, Aging, Working Set, and WSClock; they trade accuracy vs overhead.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf

A page table entry includes **R (Referenced)** and **M (Modified/Dirty)** bits: R indicates whether it has been referenced; M indicates whether it has been modified and would need write-back on eviction.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
Second-Chance replacement is FIFO plus a 'get out of jail' check: a page with its reference bit set gets a second chance instead of immediate eviction.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
Clock replacement uses a circular list with a 'hand': on page fault inspect the pointed page; if R=0 evict; if R=1 clear R and advance the hand.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
LRU (Least Recently Used) evicts the page that has not been referenced for the longest time; it is excellent conceptually but difficult to implement exactly without hardware/overhead.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
Demand paging means pages are loaded only when demanded (referenced). Locality of reference explains why this works: a process tends to use a relatively small set of pages repeatedly.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
A process’s **working set** is the set of pages it is currently using; if the working set is loaded, the process should generate few page faults.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
Prepaging is loading pages before letting the process run, attempting to reduce page faults by anticipating near-future references.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 1.pdf
The page table’s **R and M bits** are explicitly highlighted as the key per-page hardware-assisted state for replacement decisions and write-back behavior.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Page faults: MMU sees unmapped page → CPU traps to OS → OS picks a frame and may write it back to disk → OS loads the referenced page → OS updates mapping → trapped instruction restarts.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Local vs Global replacement: local policy evicts a page belonging to the faulting process; global policy may evict any process’s page (system-wide competition).
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Local vs Global framing decisions affect fairness and performance; core goals are to avoid **thrashing** and avoid **wasted memory**.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf

PFF (Page Fault Frequency) algorithm: monitor page faults per process; if above upper threshold A faults/sec the process needs more frames; if below lower threshold B faults/sec it needs fewer frames.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
If all processes are at/above the high PFF threshold, the system is likely in **thrashing**: not enough physical memory for working sets overall.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Load control techniques when memory demand exceeds physical memory include: OOM killer, swapping an entire process to storage, and cleanup methods (compaction, compression, deduplication).
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Copy-on-write: processes can share pages while reading; when a process modifies a shared page, it triggers copying so each process gets its own writable version.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Cleaning policy: a paging daemon can run mostly asleep, waking to free frames by writing dirty pages back to disk and clearing memory, improving performance by keeping clean frames available.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Page size design tradeoffs: smaller pages reduce internal fragmentation but increase page table size and TLB pressure; larger pages reduce page table size but may increase internal fragmentation.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Storage reads/writes typically happen one page at a time; page size influences I/O granularity and overhead.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Separate instruction and data spaces can use separate page tables (I-space and D-space), affecting how processes map and share code vs data.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Shared pages: processes can share instruction space; the process table may include pointers to I-space and D-space, enabling sharing and reducing memory duplication.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Shared libraries: multiple processes can use the same libraries without copying them multiple times; linking/loading strategies allow reuse in memory.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf

Implementation issues occur at: process creation (allocate memory, init page table), execution (reset MMU/clear TLB, update registers), page fault time (locate/load/evict), termination (release memory and swap usage).
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Backing store (swap space) is disk space used for paging: it may be a partition without a traditional filesystem, optimized for paging traffic; pages/processes can swap in and out of memory.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf

Page fault handling details: trap to kernel, save PC/critical registers, ISR saves registers and invokes handler; OS identifies needed virtual page; then validates address/protection before resolving the fault.
Operating Systems - Week 5 Lesson 2.pdf
Shared pages: many users run the same program; processes may share instruction space; removing a program that others share can cause page faults on later context switches if not handled correctly.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
Shared data is possible via copy-on-write: allow shared read-only mappings until a write forces a private copy.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
Backing store (swap space) can be managed as free chunks and supports swapping processes/pages in and out to extend effective memory beyond RAM.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
Segmentation: a 1D address space divided into segments that can grow/shrink independently; if one segment grows too large it can collide with others; unused allocated space impacts utilization.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
Heavyweight process: separate virtual address space and dynamically loaded code from disk; lightweight process (thread): shares address space within a process.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf

Program memory regions: Text segment contains compiled code; Data segment contains initialized globals; BSS contains uninitialized globals (zero-initialized); Free space follows for heap/stack growth (simplified view).
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
Stack: holds activation records for function calls (locals, return addresses). Heap: dynamically allocated objects that persist across calls until explicitly freed; failing to free leaks memory.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
Xinu memory allocation approach: probe memory, build table of available address blocks, pass the table to the OS being booted; the table itself is stored in memory.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
Low-level memory implementation in Xinu: all free blocks are kept on a linked list ordered by increasing address (enables coalescing/merging adjacent free blocks).
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
Xinu memory management uses memblk and memlist structures plus global pointers tracking where the heap starts/ends and other segment boundaries in the address space.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf

Key Xinu memory functions: getstk (allocate stack on create), freestk (release stack on terminate), getmem (allocate heap storage), freemem (release heap storage), meminit (initialize free list at startup).
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
meminit initializes an empty free list then scans memory to build memlist entries representing free memory blocks; this establishes the OS’s initial view of free heap memory.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf
Memory initialization also tracks OS address space segments (data, stack segments) and uses global variables to record addresses/limits used for memory management.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 1.pdf

Week 6 also covered file systems as the OS abstraction for persistent long-term storage because RAM is limited during execution and information would be lost on process termination without persistent storage.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 2.pdf
Files are OS-managed logical units supporting operations like read, write, create, delete, open, close, seek, rename, and attribute retrieval/modification.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 2.pdf
File attributes/metadata include protection, flags (read-only/hidden/etc.), time fields, and size fields; these influence OS behavior and access control.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 2.pdf
Directories provide naming/organization; path names can be absolute (/...) or relative; special entries include . and .. and ~ for home.
Operating Systems - Week 6 Lesson 2.pdf

flashcards.front: Define **Page** vs **Frame**.
flashcards.back: Page = logical block of virtual memory (virtual address space). Frame = fixed-size unit of physical RAM that holds a page.

flashcards.front: What triggers a **page fault**?
flashcards.back: The MMU detects a referenced virtual page that is unmapped/not present and traps to the OS.

flashcards.front: Write the **3-step** page fault handling outline used in class.
flashcards.back: 1) Pick a frame (evict/write-back if needed). 2) Fetch referenced page into frame + update mapping. 3) Restart trapped instruction.

flashcards.front: What is the **R bit** in a page table entry?
flashcards.back: Referenced bit: indicates whether the page has been accessed recently; used for replacement approximations (Clock/Aging).

flashcards.front: What is the **M bit** (dirty bit) and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: Modified bit: indicates page was written. If M=1, eviction usually requires writing the page back to disk first.

flashcards.front: Why is **Optimal** replacement not implementable?
flashcards.back: The OS cannot know future page references at runtime; Optimal requires future knowledge.

flashcards.front: How does **Clock** decide eviction?
flashcards.back: Inspect page at hand: if R=0 evict; if R=1 clear R and advance hand (second chance).

flashcards.front: What is **LRU**?
flashcards.back: Least Recently Used: evict the page that has not been referenced for the longest time.

flashcards.front: Why is true **LRU** hard to implement?
flashcards.back: Requires precise ordering/timestamps on every memory reference (high overhead) unless supported by hardware.

flashcards.front: What is **Demand Paging**?
flashcards.back: Pages are brought into memory only when referenced (on demand), not preloaded all at once.

flashcards.front: Define **Locality of Reference**.
flashcards.back: A process tends to reference a relatively small set of pages repeatedly in short time windows (not uniformly random).

flashcards.front: Define **Working Set**.
flashcards.back: The set of pages a process is actively using; if loaded, the process should generate few faults.

flashcards.front: What is **Prepaging**?
flashcards.back: Loading pages before running the process to reduce initial page faults by anticipating references.

flashcards.front: Local vs Global replacement (1 sentence each).
flashcards.back: Local: evict a page from the faulting process. Global: evict any process’s page system-wide.

flashcards.front: What is **PFF** (Page Fault Frequency)?
flashcards.back: A per-process control policy that monitors page faults/sec and adjusts frames allocated to each process using thresholds.

flashcards.front: PFF thresholds A and B mean what?
flashcards.back: Above A faults/sec: needs more frames. Below B faults/sec: can give up frames.

flashcards.front: What is **Thrashing**?
flashcards.back: When processes generate excessive page faults and the system spends most time paging instead of executing.

flashcards.front: What does the **paging daemon / cleaning policy** do?
flashcards.back: Runs in background to free frames by writing dirty pages to disk and keeping clean frames ready for quick allocation.

flashcards.front: Page size tradeoff: smaller pages vs larger pages.
flashcards.back: Smaller: less internal fragmentation but larger page tables and more TLB pressure. Larger: smaller page tables but more internal fragmentation.

flashcards.front: What is **Backing Store** (swap space)?
flashcards.back: Disk space used to hold pages/process images when not in RAM; used for paging/swapping.

flashcards.front: Instruction space vs Data space separation implies what?
flashcards.back: Separate page tables (I-space and D-space) can map code and data separately and enable sharing of code pages.

flashcards.front: What are **Shared Pages** in the slides?
flashcards.back: Processes can share instruction space pages; process table may track I-space and D-space pointers; enables memory savings.

flashcards.front: What are **Shared Libraries** and why useful?
flashcards.back: Multiple processes use the same library code in memory without duplicating it; linked/loaded for reuse.

flashcards.front: Heavyweight process vs Thread (lightweight process).
flashcards.back: Heavyweight: separate virtual address space. Thread: shares address space with other threads in same process.

flashcards.front: Name the core program memory segments (as taught).
flashcards.back: Text, Data, BSS, Heap, Stack (plus free space conceptually in the simplified layout).

flashcards.front: What is Xinu’s **memlist** conceptually?
flashcards.back: A linked list of free memory blocks, typically ordered by increasing address, used for allocating/freeing memory.

flashcards.front: Why order free blocks by increasing address?
flashcards.back: It makes coalescing adjacent free blocks easier when freeing memory (reduce external fragmentation).

flashcards.front: What is **meminit** in Xinu?
flashcards.back: Initializes the free list at startup by scanning memory and building memlist entries for free blocks.

flashcards.front: List the key Xinu memory functions and what each does (1 line).
flashcards.back: getstk alloc stack on create; freestk frees stack on terminate; getmem alloc heap; freemem frees heap; meminit initializes free list.

flashcards.front: File systems exist because of what 3 challenges (as taught)?
flashcards.back: RAM is limited during execution; information is lost on termination; multiple processes need concurrent access to persistent data.

quiz.question: What is the best definition of a **page frame**?
options: A logical block of virtual memory
A unit of physical memory (RAM) that holds a page
A disk sector used for swap
A CPU register storing a virtual address
quiz.explanation: A page frame is a fixed-size unit of physical RAM that stores a virtual page.

quiz.question: A **page fault** happens when:
options: The CPU cannot decode an instruction
The MMU detects an unmapped/not-present page reference and traps to the OS
The OS runs out of threads
A process calls open() on a file
quiz.explanation: Page faults are raised by the MMU on invalid/not-present page references, causing a trap to the OS.

quiz.question: Which sequence matches the class slide’s page fault handling outline?
options: Restart instruction → pick victim → load page
Pick a frame & write-back if needed → fetch referenced page & update map → restart trapped instruction
Allocate new disk partition → copy file → resume
quiz.explanation: The slide emphasizes: pick/evict, fetch/update mapping, restart instruction.

quiz.question: The **R bit** in a page table entry indicates:
options: Whether the page was referenced recently
Whether the page is readable by user-mode
Whether the page is in swap space
quiz.explanation: R = Referenced; it helps approximate recency for replacement.

quiz.question: The **M (dirty) bit** matters because:
options: If set, eviction often requires writing the page back to disk
If set, the page is always evicted first
If set, the page cannot be referenced
If set, the page table must be deleted
quiz.explanation: Dirty pages must be saved to backing store before eviction to avoid losing modifications.

quiz.question: Why is **Optimal** page replacement not implementable in a real OS at runtime?
quiz.explanation: Optimal needs perfect knowledge of the future, which the OS does not have.

quiz.question: Clock replacement chooses a victim when:
options: The page is the newest loaded
quiz.explanation: Clock evicts when it finds R=0; if R=1 it clears it and advances.

quiz.question: LRU means evict the page that:
options: Has not been referenced for the longest time
quiz.explanation: Least Recently Used = oldest last-access time.

quiz.question: Which is a correct statement about **Demand Paging**?
options: All pages are loaded into RAM before execution begins
Pages are loaded only when referenced
It requires contiguous allocation on disk
quiz.explanation: Demand paging loads pages on first use (fault-driven).

quiz.question: Locality of reference supports demand paging because:
options: Processes tend to use a small set of pages repeatedly
Processes reference pages uniformly at random
Disk is always faster than RAM
quiz.explanation: Locality implies a working set that can fit in a manageable number of frames.

quiz.question: Local replacement policy means:
options: Evict only pages from the faulting process
quiz.explanation: Local replacement confines eviction to the faulting process’s allocation.

quiz.question: Global replacement policy means:
options: Evict only pages from the faulting process
Evict pages from any process system-wide
quiz.explanation: Global replacement allows competition for frames across processes.

quiz.question: PFF (Page Fault Frequency) primarily controls:
options: Which page to evict within a process (victim choice)
How many frames each process should have (allocation across processes)
quiz.explanation: PFF adjusts per-process frame allocations based on fault rate thresholds.

quiz.question: Under PFF, if a process is above threshold A faults/sec, the OS should:
quiz.explanation: A high fault rate suggests insufficient frames for the working set.

quiz.question: Thrashing is best described as:
options: Excessive paging activity due to insufficient frames for working sets
quiz.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the system is dominated by page fault handling/paging I/O.

quiz.question: A cleaning policy / paging daemon improves performance by:
options: Keeping clean free frames available to allocate quickly
quiz.explanation: Pre-cleaned frames reduce stall time when faults require a frame immediately.

quiz.question: Smaller pages tend to:
quiz.explanation: More pages are needed to cover the same address space, so the page table grows.

quiz.question: Larger pages tend to:
quiz.explanation: The last page of a region may waste more space if the page is larger.

quiz.question: Backing store (swap space) is:
options: Disk space used to hold pages/processes when not in RAM
quiz.explanation: Swap/backing store holds evicted pages for later retrieval.

quiz.question: Xinu’s free memory management described in class keeps free blocks:
options: In a linked list ordered by increasing address
Only as a bitmap with no list
quiz.explanation: Ordered free lists help coalesce adjacent free blocks.

quiz.question: Which Xinu function initializes the free list at startup?
quiz.explanation: meminit initializes the free list and builds the memory list at boot.

quiz.question: Which pair correctly matches the Xinu functions to their role?
quiz.explanation: getmem allocates heap storage; freemem releases heap storage.

quiz.question: A heavyweight process differs from a thread (lightweight process) because:
options: It always runs in kernel mode
It has its own virtual address space, while threads share one
quiz.explanation: Processes have separate address spaces; threads share within a process.

quiz.question: Which list is the correct program memory region set taught in the slides?
quiz.explanation: Those are the canonical regions emphasized in the program layout slide.
